evening.title: What's going on with the Riemann hypothesis?
evening.text:
Last week, news broke that a mathematician had used AI to help crack one of the biggest outstanding problems in math, a proof of the Riemann hypothesis. The news follows on several other major breakthroughs in math that have either been enabled by or managed entirely by Large Language Model-based systems, a development that has left the entire field of mathematics in a state of upset.

It's too early to say much about the proof itself—mathematicians are still in the process of digesting it. But we can say a little about how the proof came about, and what it tells us about the state of math.

Tackling Riemann

The Riemann hypothesis dates from the mid-1800s and was formulated by (you will be surprised to learn) Bernhard Riemann. There's not an obvious way to describe the details of the actual hypothesis simply, but it has implications for the distribution of prime numbers. This gives it significance for areas ranging from number theory to cryptography. As Wikipedia accurately states, "It is considered by pure mathematicians to be one of the most important problems in the field."

evening.title: 'We are not ShinyHunters,' says criminal hacking crew that looks and acts just like ShinyHunters
evening.text:
Inception, a new data theft and extortion gang that security researchers have theorized is a rebrand of the ShinyHunters group, “reject[s] this attribution” and claims it has no affiliation with any prior cybercrime enterprise.

In a lengthy statement posted Tuesday and shared on X, the extortionists insist that they are a new group, with new operators, and that their alleged social engineering attacks aren’t copying anyone - but rather just abusing the weakest link in an organization’s security: “a human being holding a phone.”

The rant follows a Monday report by Okta Threat Intelligence - along with social media speculation since Inception’s inception last week - that the newly emerged group is very likely ShinyHunters with a different name.

Okta’s researchers based their analysis on the two groups’ shared infrastructure, plus Inception’s nearly identical tactics: voice phishing, during which the scammers trick targets into entering credentials into phishing pages and approving multi-factor authentication (MFA) requests.

Inception apparently took offense to this. “We would like to address this once, clearly, and only once,” the crims' statement says. “We are not ShinyHunters. We were never ShinyHunters. We are Inception.”

The gang argues that its overlapping domain registrars, hosting providers, and DNS services don’t prove anything. These are commodity services, “available to anyone who can pay for them,” Inception wrote.

Plus, their similar methodologies don't necessarily make Inception a reboot. “That is not theft of tradecraft,” they wrote. “It is acknowledgment of a good idea – the same way every group after LockBit used a leak site, and nobody called them LockBit.”

“Inception is a new group, with new operators, our own objectives, and our own name,” the statement continues. “What we share with the past is plumbing.”

To be fair, the new crime crew has every reason to distance itself from ShinyHunters.

That gang’s September FBI hack - plus several earlier digital heists during which the criminals stole information belonging to millions of people, including cancer patients, university and K-12 students - put a massive target on its collective backs.

And while at least three ShinyHunters suspects were arrested in September and October, there's no confirmation that authorities have dismantled the entire operation.

Plus, as a ShinyHunters spokesperson told The Register in an earlier interview, they and others in the crew started off as GnosticPlayers before rebranding as ShinyHunters in 2020 - so a reboot isn’t beyond the realm of possibility.

Inception, for its part, says it “will not comment further on the ghost of ShinyHunters,” and it has its own work to do. And by work, it means copying ShinyHunters' playbook, stealing corporate data, and extorting victim companies for massive sums of money.®

evening.title: Back-to-back measles deaths is our new reality; US tally now at 14
evening.text:
Last week, international health authorities formally announced that the US had lost its measles-elimination status, meaning that the virus is once again endemic. But the official determination is a bit like getting the technical readout of a cracked dam while the country is already feet under water.

The national tally of measles cases is nearing 6,000 for the year, the highest count since 1991. Transmission is widespread, with 47 states and jurisdictions reporting cases. There have been 43 outbreaks this year, which account for 96 percent of the cases. Four states have case counts above 500, including Pennsylvania, which leads with 1,638 cases as of November 23. Nearly 650 people have been hospitalized nationwide. As of today, 14 people have died.

Deaths and transmission

On November 23, Pennsylvania's health department announced its ninth confirmed death, an unvaccinated resident of Centre County. On November 24, Wisconsin reported its third measles death, an adult in Lafayette County. The report follows two other deaths in the state, an infant and a child. New York has also reported a death, which was of a 7-month-old baby. On November 20, Virginia reported the death of a young child between the age of 0 and 4.

evening.title: FireAnt Mini Uncrewed Ground Vehicles Deploy Drone Detection Sensors In U.S. Army Test
evening.text:
A FireAnt uncrewed ground vehicle (UGV) was used to deploy small sensors capable of detecting hostile drones on the ground during a recent U.S. Army test exercise. Using UGVs to quickly establish even localized sensor networks could give Army units a valuable, if not increasingly critical, boost in situational awareness of potential threats in the air and on the ground.

The sensor-toting FireAnt was among the capabilities demonstrated during the U.S. Army-led Needs-Driven Acquisition for Near-Term Operations Accelerated Capability II (NANO ACE II) event in October. The service only recently shared details about NANO ACE II, which took place at the Multidomain Training Area (MDTA) in Tan-Tan, Morocco, in cooperation with that country’s armed forces. The larger NANO ACE effort falls under the broader umbrella of the Army’s Operation Jailbreak, which has been focused primarily on devising new networking capabilities to link disparate systems.

“NANO ACE tested prototype systems that combine autonomous platforms with different payloads, mission management software and robust communications,” according to an Army release. “This test aimed to evaluate semi-autonomous capability sets that extend C-UAS [counter-uncrewed aerial systems] coverage and addressed an emergent U.S. joint force requirement to field integrated, autonomous sensing and effector capabilities on an accelerated acquisition timeline.”

“To meet these objectives, industry developers evaluated their systems against strict operational criteria, testing whether the platforms could operate independently on unimproved terrain while surviving a contested electronic warfare environment,” the release added. “Hosting this evaluation at the Moroccan owned MDTA underscores a deep appreciation for the Kingdom of Morocco’s ongoing partnership. AMTEC [the U.S. Army’s Africa Multi-Domain Training and Experimentation Center] is intended to leverage the region’s open electromagnetic spectrum, uncongested airspace and contested terrain to help combined forces test emerging technologies and maintain a decisive advantage in a complex strategic environment.”

In addition to AMTEC, representatives from the Army’s Global Tactical Edge Acquisition Directorate, the Army Test and Evaluation Command (ATEC), U.S. Army Central (ARCENT), U.S. Africa Command (AFRICOM), the Army’s Southern European Task Force-Africa (SETAF-AF), and an unnamed “tactical U.S. Army division” participated in the event in Morocco.

Produced by Swarmbotics AI, FireAnt is a small 4×4 UGV designed to be readily reconfigurable for a wide variety of missions, including electronic warfare, surveillance and reconnaissance, and even being used as a one-way-attack munition. FireAnts are also capable of being employed in semi-autonomous swarms.

Pictures accompanying the Army’s release about NANO ACE II show the FireAnt configured to carry six small ground sensors, three each on two sets of rails angled to either side. The sensors slide off the rails and come to rest on a trio of small legs.

How the sensors in question function is not immediately clear, but they have a spherical central body and a slender antenna mast that extends upward. Sensors of this size and configuration could detect drones in various ways, including passively picking up signals they emit or by registering their acoustic signature.

As an aside, another FireAnt was spotted at a separate Army test exercise recently conducted at Fort Hood in Texas with what looks to be another type of deployable sensor system called Maple Seeds. These are “low-power, lightweight, disposable RF [radiofrequency]” sensors that “can locate, differentiate, and track targets in deep fires areas in contested A2/AD [anti-access/area denial] environments,” according to manufacturer MaXentric Technologies.

A separate version of FireAnt with a fixed acoustic sensor array has also been developed for NANO ACE, but it is not clear if it has been demonstrated at one of the Army’s test exercises yet.

Depending on how they are networked together, ground sensors deployed via UGV, as well as UGVs with their own sensor packages, could provide multiple streams of data for operators to fuse together. This, in turn, would help build a higher-fidelity picture of potential drone threats. That data could then be used to cue other more capable sensors to further track and categorize those objects of interest, as well as effectors to engage them. Ukrainian forces have notably been employing broadly similar kinds of distributed, multi-layered sensor architectures to spot incoming drone attacks and manage resources to respond to them for years now.

Using UGVs in this role also opens new options for deploying ground sensors in forward areas while also reducing risks to human operators. A swarm of sensor-toting robotic vehicles would be able to seed that coverage across a broader area faster. Army testing earlier this year involving a Bradley Fighting Vehicle acting as a carrier for FireAnts demonstrated how UGVs could be brought to forward areas before pushing ahead of friendly forces, regardless of what their assigned tasks might be.

There’s a cost component to this equation, too. Whether seeded via UGV or other means, unattended ground sensors offer a lower-cost option for expanding coverage, especially in areas where it would be too risky to deploy more conventional radars and other assets. If they operate passively, the sensors themselves could be challenging for enemy forces to find and neutralize them once they’re in place.

While the recent NANO ACE event in Morocco was focused on counter-drone capabilities, sensors deployed in this way could be used to detect potential threats on the ground, as well. It’s understandable, though, that the Army is most interested currently in providing units new ways to spot incoming uncrewed attackers, a threat ecosystem that is only continuing to expand in scale and scope. Soldiers can expect drone attacks to come at the tactical edge, in rear areas, and everywhere in between in future conflicts.

Recent experiences from the war with Iran, as well as other conflicts in the Middle East and ongoing fighting in Ukraine, have shown that various tiers of uncrewed attackers can easily be layered in with other weapons and approach targets from multiple vectors simultaneously. In Ukraine, a tactic has also emerged where human operators fly small first-person-view kamikaze drones to forward areas where they then lie in wait on the ground like remotely-operated land mines. All of this only increases challenges for defenders when it comes to just spotting threats, let alone prioritizing and engaging them.

It should also be stressed here that unattended ground sensors are in no way new to the U.S. military. Historically, fixed-wing aircraft, helicopters, and small teams on the ground have been used to emplace them. The best-known example of this is Operation Igloo White, the then-state-of-the-art Vietnam War effort to remotely monitor movement along the Ho Chi Minh Trail. Igloo White also proved to be controversial due to its cost, complexity, and mixed results.

The Army and other branches of the U.S. military have also previously experimented with using uncrewed aerial systems to deploy sensors on the ground in forward areas, as well as act as readily relocatable sensor nodes themselves. The service has raised the possibility of using high-altitude balloons for this purpose, as well.

There are still potential hurdles for the Army to clear before it can employ UGV-deployed ground sensors on a broader scale. As noted, NANO ACE is an offshoot of Operation Jailbreak, and networking all of these nodes together could present challenges. Army officials have also talked in the past about how expanding distributed sensor coverage can produce data overload.

“One of the big problems we identified in this particular scenario is going to be we have too much data, and we haven’t been able to correlate it in the way that we want to provide it to the warfighter,” now-retired Lt. Gen. Scott McKean, then Project Convergence experiment director and deputy commander of Army Futures Command, said following a test exercise back in 2022. “A few years ago, we wouldn’t have had that problem because we weren’t even talking to each other, and our machines certainly wouldn’t be talking to each other. And so that’s a huge step forward, the fact that we are all sharing data. … We have the capability right now to take multiple communication pathways. Some of those are very military-specific. Some of those are actually quite commercial. And we can use those in multiple ways, so if one is denied, we switch to another one.”

“We still need to keep working on how we standardize the data so that we’re all able to access it and we’re all able to share it across services and platforms,” then-Secretary of the Army Christine Wormuth also said at the time. “I think we’re making progress on that, but there’s still work that has to be done. … We’re now able to tap into a huge volume of data. A lot of the challenge is going to be figuring out how we process that as quickly as we can, and I think we did see some real improvements in terms of how quickly we were able to take information and change it into what I would call more actionable knowledge. The other thing I think we have to do is commanders are going to have to figure out what are the critical information requirements that they need.”

These are areas where developments in artificial intelligence and machine learning could help human operators sift through the data.

The Army has also struggled with attempts to field larger uncrewed platforms in recent years. This stands in the face of global trends, especially in Ukraine, where smaller UGVs have steadily become a fixture in the ongoing conflict.

FireAnt increasingly looks to be at the forefront of Army efforts to integrate UGVs of various types into its broader force structure. The recent NANO ACE II event has highlighted another potentially important role for these uncrewed platforms as a way to help commanders get a better sense of the battlespace around them in the air and on the ground.

evening.title: Sweden’s Gripens Are Doing Big Things With A Tiny Footprint In Poland
evening.text:
Russian cruise missiles enter Polish airspace during a major attack on Ukraine. NATO fighters scramble. Two Swedish Gripens join Polish F-16s in the response, tracking airborne threats over Poland. One Swedish pilot attempts to intercept an object believed to be a Russian Kh-101 cruise missile and has conditional NATO authorization to engage. But exceptionally difficult weather prevents positive identification, and the pilot holds fire.

The incident on November 20 highlights the operational value of Sweden’s small forward presence at the airbase of Mińsk Mazowiecki, outside Warsaw. Just two days earlier, TWZ made an exclusive visit to the base, where Sweden is supporting NATO air operations with a forward team of just eight personnel. The Gripens themselves remain primarily based in Sweden, but the small forward support element provides an additional operating location that can help sustain missions on very short notice and give the Swedish fighters greater flexibility as they scramble to defend NATO’s eastern flank.

The operation is a practical illustration of Sweden’s effort to extend its long-established dispersed fighter operations concept across NATO — not as a future capability waiting to be validated, but as an operational approach continuously evolving through real-world missions.

“The events of the past few days have demonstrated the operational value of the concepts we have been developing,” Major General Jonas Wikman, chief of the Swedish Air Force, tells TWZ. “In both Poland and Finland, Swedish fighters have responded rapidly and decisively alongside our allies, while maintaining our national alert commitment.”

“In Poland, we conducted a demanding air defense mission lasting several hours under very challenging conditions. Our small forward support element was instrumental in enabling us to sustain that operation.”

Wikman is particularly proud of the personnel involved, describing the professionalism, judgement, and resolve demonstrated by Swedish personnel in the air and on the ground.

“We are not developing these concepts for some future scenario. We are using them in real-world operations today, learning from every mission and continuously improving our ability to defend our shared airspace. That is what being ready means to me.”

Expanding the Swedish model deeper into NATO

Sweden has spent roughly 60 years building its air arm around the ability to operate fighters from locations beyond their normal air bases, including road strips, civilian airports, and the strategic island of Gotland. The approach is focused on moving aircraft and support personnel quickly, limiting their exposure and avoiding dependence on a small number of large, fixed installations. They are truly masters of dispersed operations, and everything is designed to operate with a minimal logistics and manpower footprint. It turns out that this Cold War concept of operations is more relevant today than it has been in decades.

Now, Sweden is adapting that model to NATO operations, while other air forces are replicating it out of necessity.

“We are really ambitious about our NATO operations, our integration into NATO, and our role as a security provider within the alliance,” Wikman says.

The Swedish Air Force has already deployed fighters to NATO missions in Iceland and Poland, while also maintaining national commitments. Wikman describes the broader effort as an evolution of Sweden’s dispersed operations concept, incorporating the flexibility associated with the U.S. Air Force’s Agile Combat Employment (ACE) while extending the ability to operate from locations across allied territory.

The scale of the current Polish deployment marks a significant change from an earlier operation at Malbork, where Sweden sent more than 100 personnel.

Wikman wanted to reduce that footprint substantially, challenging the wing commander to determine how little personnel and equipment were actually required to support the mission.

The result was a forward team of just eight personnel.

Rather than establishing a substantial forward operating base, the team uses familiar Swedish equipment and procedures, bringing what is required to support aircraft operating from Sweden. The approach is intended to be repeatable, reducing the preparation and logistical burden associated with deployments and making it easier to shift support between different NATO directions.

Wikman believes the concept can make operations more flexible, allowing Sweden to sustain commitments in different locations without having to build a large support organization for each one.

The Missed Refueling Base

The forward location in Poland is described as a Missed Refueling Base, or MRB. Originally established as a contingency option, it has proven sufficiently useful to become routinely used for forward Gripen operations, including for scheduled turnarounds (landing, basic service/refuel, and departure) of the jets.

Gripens normally operate from Swedish bases, even when patrolling over Polish skies, and can use air-to-air refueling to extend their time and reach. The MRB provides another option if an aircraft needs to land, whether because of an unexpected issue or as part of a planned operation.

A problem with the refueling probe, for example, could prevent an aircraft from receiving fuel in the air. Having a forward location available means the aircraft can recover without necessarily having to return to its home base in Sweden.

But its broader value is not simply emergency recovery.

The location extends operational reach, flexibility, and the number of options available to commanders. Aircraft can land, refuel, and receive limited maintenance, and even rearm during a crisis, with the tiny forward team providing a means of sustaining operations without deploying a full squadron support infrastructure.

The Swedish approach is built around the idea that an operating location does not need to replicate a home air base to provide significant operational value.

The Gripen itself is famously designed for rapid servicing. Wikman says an aircraft in the air-to-air role can be refueled and rearmed in less than 15 minutes using one officer and five conscripts. That combination of aircraft design, procedures, and personnel is central to the Swedish model.

Tankers, turnaround and surviving the targeting cycle

The MRB also ties into Sweden’s thinking about how fighters will operate in a high-intensity conflict.

Air-to-air refueling remains valuable, but Wikman stresses that Sweden must be able to conduct operations without depending on tanker availability. Tankers could be heavily tasked, unavailable, or threatened in a contested environment.

The objective is not to abandon aerial refueling, but to ensure it is not a single point of failure.

“We intend to do the quick refueling within the enemy targeting cycle,” Wikman says, describing the importance of being able to land, refuel, and get back into the air quickly, frustrating an adversary’s efforts to detect and successfully attack those same aircraft while they sit on their airfield.

Sweden is also developing procedures for hot rearming, allowing weapons to be replenished as aircraft are turned around without the engine shutting down. Wikman expects this process to take less than 10 minutes, potentially around five or six minutes, although the procedures continue to evolve.

The challenge becomes more complex as the distance between operating locations and logistical support grows.

As Sweden develops the ability to disperse fighters and operate farther from its main bases, it must also develop the logistics to sustain aircraft, personnel, fuel, ammunition, and maintenance across those same distances. Extending operational reach without extending the supporting supply system would ultimately limit the value of the concept.

That is an important area for continued development within NATO, particularly as nations seek to make dispersed operations sustainable rather than simply achievable for short periods.

Finland, Poland and national QRA simultaneously

The Polish deployment is taking place alongside Swedish support for air defense operations in Finland and Sweden’s own national quick reaction alert (QRA) mission.

In Finland, Sweden has trained Finnish maintenance personnel at each wing to support Gripen hot refueling. The Finnish personnel have also received virtual-reality training equipment to help them maintain their skills.

Wikman describes the Finnish arrangement as more bilateral in nature, while the Polish deployment is part of Sweden’s effort to establish a repeatable way of operating across NATO. At the same time, the involvement of the Gripens speaks to the situation in Poland, where jets are scrambling from Sweden to deal with growing airspace incursions by Russian drones and cruise missiles. They execute this mission alongside Polish F-16s and other NATO fighters based, even if temporarily, in Poland and the wider region.

At the same time, Sweden is maintaining its national QRA commitment. Wikman said the effort is centered on Ronneby, in southern Sweden, but draws on aircraft and pilots from other wings, including Luleå, close to the Arctic Circle.

“More or less three directions: Finland, Poland, and our national QRA at the same time, which is a new kind of record for us,” he says.

For a relatively small air force with six fighter squadrons, sustaining those commitments is a significant undertaking. Of those squadrons, more than one is also pretty busy with introducing the new Gripen E version. The smaller Polish footprint is intended to make that kind of activity more manageable, allowing personnel to rotate without maintaining a much larger deployed contingent.

The approach also allows Sweden to concentrate on generating fighter sorties while relying on forward support locations to provide flexibility when operational circumstances demand it.

Lessons from Ukraine

Wikman sees a close connection between Sweden’s approach and the way Ukraine has had to operate its air force under sustained Russian attack.

He says the Swedish and Ukrainian air forces are aligned in their thinking about dispersed operations, and that the relationship has shifted rapidly from one of support to partnership. Ukrainian experience is now feeding back into Swedish thinking.

“This fits Ukraine perfectly,” Wikman says, pointing to the value of movement, dispersal and the ability to continue operating despite an adversary’s efforts to target air bases.

Wikman draws a distinction between preparing for a conflict and conducting one under fire.

“They are fighting the fight. We prepared the fight.”

Ukraine’s need to keep aircraft moving between locations and avoid predictable operating patterns has demonstrated the importance of dispersal in practice. For Sweden, those lessons reinforce an approach it has developed over decades, while also highlighting the need to make it work with allies and partners.

Indeed, the Gripen has frequently been promoted as a particularly suitable fighter for Ukraine because its design and support concept are built around these kinds of operations, including the ability to operate from austere locations with small ground crews and rapid turnaround. Kyiv is scheduled to receive its first of up to 16 Gripen C/D fighters early next year, with longer-term plans calling for more advanced Gripen Es to join the Ukrainian Air Force, too.

For now, the Polish Gripen deployment is a modest operation in terms of personnel and equipment, but that is precisely the point. Sweden is demonstrating how a small support element, backed by aircraft and deeper maintenance capacity at home, can extend the reach of its fighters without recreating a full air base abroad.

And now, with Swedish Gripens responding to real airspace threats over Poland, the value of that approach is no longer theoretical.

The longer-term challenge will be sustaining the model across different NATO locations, with host-nation support, ammunition access, fuel, maintenance, and common procedures needed for more demanding operations.

For Wikman, however, the process is already underway.

Sweden is not waiting for the next conflict to determine how its dispersed fighter operations will work across NATO. It is learning, adapting, and refining the concept while flying the missions that make it necessary.

evening.title: Turkish Kizilelma Fighter Drone Declared Operational
evening.text:
Turkish drone manufacturer Baykar says it has made aviation history, announcing that the first three of its Bayraktar Kizilelma uncrewed combat aircraft have entered the inventory of the Turkish security forces following the completion of acceptance testing. The company describes the development as the first operational induction of an uncrewed ‘fighter jet’ anywhere in the world.

It is a significant milestone for a program that has progressed from its initial unveiling in 2021 to flight testing, weapons integration, and now military acceptance. Baykar says the program has accumulated approximately 600 test and training sorties.

But the significance of Kizilelma goes beyond the question of whether it represents a world first. The aircraft belongs to an emerging category of uncrewed combat aircraft that is increasingly difficult to describe using the traditional Uncrewed Combat Air Vehicle (UCAV) label. Unlike conventional armed drones, Kizilelma was designed for fighter-type missions, including air-to-air combat.

It arrives on the scene as the United States, China, Australia and European countries pursue their own concepts for fighter-like uncrewed aircraft intended to operate in increasingly demanding combat environments, especially alongside crewed fighters.

Beyond the traditional UCAV

The term UCAV encompasses a broad range of aircraft, but is typically applied to more sophisticated, stealthy, jet-powered aircraft intended to penetrate defended airspace and to conduct air-to-ground attack, as well as electronic attack and surveillance and reconnaissance (it is worth noting that some still refer to any weaponized complex drone system capable of sizable endurance and delivery of ordnance as UCAVs). Regardless, the ability of many UCAV concepts to carry guided bombs and missiles does not necessarily make them fighter drones in the conventional sense.

A different concept is now emerging: uncrewed aircraft specifically designed to undertake fighter missions, and especially air-to-air combat.

Within this narrower category, another important distinction is the Collaborative Combat Aircraft (CCA). These are designed to operate alongside crewed combat aircraft, extending their sensor coverage, weapons capacity, and tactical flexibility. Their employment involves considerable autonomy, but they are generally conceived as part of a wider crewed-uncrewed combat formation.

Kizilelma sits somewhere between these concepts. It is intended to undertake fighter-type missions, including air-to-air combat, but is also expected to perform air-to-ground missions and eventually operate as part of a wider crewed-uncrewed team.

Its design and intended employment make it particularly fighter-like among the emerging generation of advanced uncrewed combat aircraft.

Kizilelma’s fighter credentials

Kizilelma was conceived with a rather different premise from most UCAVs. It is claimed the aircraft will be capable of supersonic performance in later versions and is tailored for missions typically undertaken by crewed fighter jets.

In particular, it is intended to complement Turkey’s next-generation TF Kaan crewed fighter. While it incorporates a degree of reduced observability, stealth was not the overriding design driver. Baykar is also pursuing a naval variant capable of operating from ships with short flight decks.

The basic aircraft has a reported maximum speed of Mach 0.9, a cruise speed of Mach 0.6, and a payload capacity of approximately 3,000 pounds. Other specifications include a maximum endurance exceeding three hours, a typical mission radius of 500 nautical miles, a service ceiling of 40,000 feet, and an operational altitude of 25,000 feet.

These characteristics place it closer to a light fighter than to the majority of UCAVs developed to date, which tend to prioritize endurance, payload capacity, and reduced observability over fighter-like performance.

One of the program’s most significant milestones came in November 2025, when a Kizilelma used a domestically developed Gökdoğan air-to-air missile to strike a jet-powered aerial target.

The target was designated using Aselsan’s Murad active electronically scanned array (AESA) radar. The engagement demonstrated the integration of an uncrewed aircraft, onboard radar, and beyond-visual-range missile in an air-to-air engagement.

The aircraft has also demonstrated autonomous formation flight. In December 2025, two Kizilelma prototypes reportedly flew in close formation using intelligent fleet autonomy. A subsequent formation flight alongside Italian M-346 aircraft in May 2026 represented another step toward crewed-uncrewed teaming.

Nevertheless, the extent to which the aircraft can independently detect, identify, track, and engage hostile aircraft remains unclear.

The international race to develop uncrewed fighters

Kizilelma is not emerging in isolation. Several countries are now pursuing related concepts, although their designs, operational philosophies and levels of maturity differ.

The United States is pursuing its uncrewed fighter concept through the Air Force’s Collaborative Combat Aircraft program.

In March 2025, the U.S. Air Force formally designated General Atomics’ YFQ-42A and Anduril’s YFQ-44A as uncrewed fighters.

Both aircraft are intended to operate alongside crewed fighters, with the aim of extending their combat effectiveness through additional sensors, weapons and autonomous capabilities.

The program has progressed considerably. In June 2026, the Air Force awarded production contracts for both designs, while the YFQ-44A conducted an AIM-120 AMRAAM firing test against a target in July.

The first aircraft were subsequently delivered to the service’s Experimental Operations Unit in September, where they are being used to develop operating concepts, tactics, and procedures.

The American approach differs somewhat from Kizilelma. The CCA aircraft are being developed entirely around collaborative operations with crewed platforms, rather than as independent uncrewed fighters with collaborative capabilities.

Nevertheless, they are part of the same broader shift toward aircraft capable of undertaking increasingly demanding fighter missions without an onboard pilot.

Meanwhile, China has made considerable progress with its stealthy GJ-11 Mysterious Dragon UCAV.

The People’s Liberation Army Air Force announced that the GJ-11 had entered service in November 2025, predating Kizilelma’s delivery by approximately a year.

Recent Chinese state media coverage has provided additional insight into the GJ-11’s intended operational role, including air-to-ground strikes, suppression of enemy air defenses, and operations alongside crewed J-16 and J-20 fighters.

However, the publicly disclosed mission set remains primarily focused on air-to-surface operations. There has been no comparable public demonstration of the GJ-11 conducting an air-to-air missile engagement against an aerial target.

That does not establish that the aircraft lacks such a capability. Its precise performance and operational role remain difficult to determine given the limited transparency surrounding China’s uncrewed combat aviation programs. Still, this is a more traditional UCAV, built around low observability, range, and payload, not fighter-like performance.

China is developing a broader family of CCAs, reflecting an approach that extends beyond the GJ-11 and increasingly emphasizes the integration of uncrewed systems into fighter formations with higher-performance designs. We have seen China testing these daily in satellite images. They are larger uncrewed aircraft and much more like Turkey’s offering than America’s CCAs or traditional UCAVs.

European manufacturers are also pursuing the next generation of uncrewed combat aircraft, some of which are similar to Kizilelma in basic concept.

Sweden’s Saab, for instance, is exploring autonomous combat aircraft and crewed-uncrewed teaming as part of its longer-term combat aviation development, including a large fighter-like uncrewed design. Airbus’ Wingman drone is also of the same fighter-like general design family.

Meanwhile, in Australia, Boeing’s MQ-28 Ghost Bat CCA is also making strides. Only weeks after the Kizilelma test-fired an air-to-air missile, Boeing made a first live-fire weapons shot from a Ghost Bat drone, with an AIM-120 Advanced Medium-Range Air-to-Air Missile (AMRAAM) launched over the sprawling Woomera Range Complex (WRC) in southern Australia. The milestone event comes as the Australian government committed further to the Ghost Bat program and collaborative air capabilities in general. Although dropped from German plans for now, Boeing has reported strong export interest in the drone.

So clearly, these larger, fighter-like, higher-performance UAV designs are of increasing interest globally, and Kizilelma was really the first to emerge, establishing this unique segment of the drone space.

What does being operational actually mean?

Baykar’s announcement confirms that the first three Kizilelma aircraft completed acceptance testing and entered the inventory of Turkish security forces.

However, several important questions remain unanswered.

The company has not publicly identified the receiving military branch. Janes reported that imagery of the occasion showed an officer believed to belong to the Turkish Land Forces Command.

More importantly, delivery and acceptance do not necessarily mean that Kizilelma has achieved full operational capability.

Its readiness for combat, initial operational mission set, and the extent to which its air-to-air weapons capabilities have been cleared for operational use remain unclear.

The autonomy question is equally important. Autonomous formation flight and a successful radar-guided missile engagement are significant achievements, but neither establishes that the aircraft can independently, or even semi-autonomously, conduct the complete fighter engagement process in a real combat environment. The aircraft can rely on man-in-the-loop control (where a pilot is physically flying it like an MQ-9 Reaper) and still carry out various missions, but a larger degree of autonomy would unlock greater flexibility, resilience due to less reliance on high-bandwidth datalinks, and far more efficient pairing with crewed assets.

A new category of combat aircraft

Regardless of whether Baykar’s world-first assertion withstands closer scrutiny, Kizilelma’s entry into Turkish military inventory is an important development in the evolution of uncrewed combat aviation.

The aircraft represents a move away from the traditional model of uncrewed aircraft as primarily persistent surveillance and strike platforms, toward systems intended to undertake some of the most demanding missions in modern air warfare.

The United States, China, Turkey, Australia and several European countries are pursuing their own approaches to this challenge.

Whether it becomes a true independent uncrewed fighter, a collaborative wingman to the TF Kaan or a platform capable of fulfilling both roles remains to be seen, but efforts to realize those aspirations will certainly accelerate over the coming years. This is especially the case now that the program can build operational experience with the active Turkish armed forces.

evening.title: Arm strongarms site that hosts ad-free documentation and it may disappear
evening.text:
Arm is swinging the hammer at an enthusiast’s site hosting a bloat-free version of its instruction reference documentation, demanding it be taken offline after several years of availability.

The demand from Arm lawyers to Jon Palmisciano concern Jon’s Arm Reference, a site that provides the same arm Instruction Set Architecture (ISA) info available on Arm’s site, but with what Palmisciano describes as “without a million popups and all of the bloat” that Arm provides on its own.

According to Palmisciano, his copy of the Arm ISA was culled from machine-readable XML files and stripped of the bloat. He built his version in 2022 with new CSS on top of it, and the addition of a quick search feature that, according to his comments on Hacker News, isn’t available in the official version.

“The aim has always been to make it the most comfortable and bullshit-free browsing experience for people who need these docs daily,” Palmisciano wrote in HN. Based on the responses the site seems to have plenty of fans.

That doesn’t matter to Arm, though: As far as the lawyers are concerned, Palmisciano’s site is a copyright violation due to its use of Arm trademarks and inclusion of copyrighted reference material for the Armv9-A and Armv9-A architecture.

Arm doesn’t care if Palmisciano’s project is well intentioned or for the benefit of the many software developers that write code for its chipsets, either: They want it offline by December 4 – 10 days from the publication of this story – or else.

As for what is going to happen, it seems like Jon’s Arm Reference will likely cease to exist in a little over a week – at least in its current form.

“Ideally I'd love to just get permission from Arm to keep the site up, but I'm pretty pessimistic about that,” Palmisciano told us. That said, Palmisciano has “already seen a few archives and mirrors already.” The HN thread discussing the takedown order includes links to several versions, and Palmisciano has another trick up his sleeve that he’s considering playing: Open-sourcing the software he used to build his ISA page.

“I'd also consider open-sourcing my tooling so that people can (for their own private use) turn the original XML downloads from Arm into an identical site they can host locally,” Palmisciano told us. He said that he'll likely tweet about opening the tooling if he does do so. He's also considered directing the URL for Jon's Arm reference to point to the open-source tool, but Arm wants the subdomain it's hosted on removed from his site as well, so that may not happen.

Arm has been in touch to defend itself as well, saying that Arm appreciates the efforts of people like Palmisciano, but that it still has to protect its brand, and documentation.

"We have a responsibility to ensure Arm is the primary source of technical resources and information and to protect the Arm brand," an Arm spokesperson told us. "Striking the right balance between third parties sharing helpful peer-to-peer resources while ensuring copyrighted Arm-related technical content is accurate has been critical to building the thriving ecosystem we have today."

In other words, if you’re an Arm dev worried about losing a valuable resource and having to turn to a website that bombards you with junk just to look up a few simple opcodes and operands you’d better find a backup host before next month.

That said, Arm is willing to work something out with Palmisciano, the company told us.

"We have recently flagged our concerns with regard to the use of Arm copyright content and the Arm brand on this website and shared the Arm trademark guidelines," Arm explained. "Our hope is to open a constructive dialogue, and we've asked that the website owner reach out as we seek to resolve this."

As Palmisciano posted on HN, Arm is asking for removal of its trademark and copyrighted documentation. That, Palmisciano said, "seems hard to work around while still keeping the site useful." He also followed up around 8.30 pm GMT on Tuesday to let us know that he has not yet heard directly from Arm. ®

evening.title: An AI coding agent, a browser, and a Mac tool found a financial firm's access key in under 6 minutes
evening.text:
A Romanian hacker, armed with only an open source coding agent, a Chrome browser, and a Mac, tried multiple ways to break into a financial services firm, ultimately found an access key - luckily, it was a decoy - and carried out an entire (almost) attack in under six minutes.

It’s a stark reminder that miscreants don’t need sophisticated malware - as in the Binance heist - or AI pen-testing tools like ARTEX to carry out intrusions into critical networks. Open source coding agents, and specifically OpenCode in this case, also work just fine.

“What surprised me most was how little it took and the toolkit: a free coding agent, the curl that comes with every Mac and an ordinary Chrome, all from one laptop,” Jesta co-founder and CTO Lior Finkelshtein told The Register. “Until now I thought that we had more time until tools like OpenCode are used in offensive operations. This incident shows us that it's already in use in the field, and we will probably see more of that in the future.”

Jesta is a Tel Aviv-based security startup that builds defensive tools to detect and stop autonomous AI attacks. In a report shared exclusively with The Register, Finkelshtein documented an attempted intrusion targeting a major financial services company that’s also a Jesta customer - the security shop declined to say which one.

Jesta’s investigation into the incident determined that someone in Bucharest downloaded a free AI coding agent called OpenCode and pointed it at the financial services customer on November 16 at 4:24:57 a.m. ET.

'Nothing in OpenCode was built for hacking'

OpenCode is an open source coding agent that lets users connect to more than 200 model providers or local models, including Anthropic’s Claude models, OpenAI’s GPTs, Google’s Gemini, DeepSeek, and Z.ai’s GLM. Jesta doesn’t know which model the attacker used, as there was nothing in the traffic that named the model. OpenCode's web fetch tool, however, did name itself, so Jesta knows the attacker used this coding agent - not a scanner - to do the dirty work.

“Nothing in OpenCode was built for hacking,” Finkelshtein said in a Tuesday report about the agent-led attack. But, he added, nothing in the coding agent “stops you from pointing it at someone else's website either. When you do, the agent goes through the site the same way it goes through code. It reads, tries something, reads the result and tries the next thing, for as long as you let it run.”

That’s what it did in this operation, which took less than six minutes and cost the human operator nothing.

The first call came from a Chrome browser on a Mac, requesting the front page of one of the financial firm’s systems. The site refused it, and six seconds later, the same IPv6 address in Bucharest, on an ordinary DIGI Romania business line, tried again. It used the same Chrome version, but said it was an Android Pixel 10 phone (it wasn’t) to see if the site would let a phone in (it didn’t).

After failing to gain access through the front page, the agent asked the system for its API definition, which was also refused. Five seconds later, it tried a different address - this one was a decoy set up by Jesta - and it answered the agent, providing the readable file defining how the API works.

The agent read the document, and 13 seconds later followed a link it contained. At 4:26:01 a.m. ET, Jesta’s defenses marked the website visitor as an AI agent, opened a case, and from here on out, everything the agent accessed was contained inside a fake environment designed to trick intruders. This included a phony key, which the attacker then used to attempt to break into the company’s systems.

“It worked like a developer,” Finkelshtein said about the coding agent. “It read the API docs and did what they said. It found a key and used it. It checked whether the lock was real, then made up a key of its own and tried that. None of the threat feeds the customer has knew the address, so a blocklist would never have stopped it. The bar for doing this is now installing an app. Think about how many people can do that.”

'No blocklist would have helped'

In addition to OpenCode, the attacker used only Chrome 157, both in desktop and mobile modes, and curl/8.7.1, a command-line tool that has shipped with every Mac since macOS 15. The agent passed information between the three tools. It included the planted key in a command-line request and then tested three scenarios – using the decoy key, no key, and a fabricated key – to determine whether what it found in the API documentation was legit.

It also tried multiple URLs using the browser. While it ultimately identified a valid endpoint, it attempted to read from one that accepts only data submissions, so its request was blocked again. Five minutes and 44 seconds after the first request, it gave up, and the logs haven’t detected any activity from this same intruder since then.

The security shop and its customer disclosed the activity to law enforcement and told us it’s “being handled.”

While the attacker wasn’t able to steal anything in this attempt, security teams still need to take note, according to Finkelshtein.

“No blocklist would have helped” detect the malicious traffic, he explained. “Most security tools still decide by asking whether an address is known to be bad, and for this one the answer was no. If that key had been real, it would have been in.”

Instead of blocklists, Finkelshtein suggests paying attention to what the visitor does. In this case, several of its actions gave it away - including following a link that only existed inside an API doc, using a desktop browser and a fake phone, then curl, all from the same address within minutes, and trying multiple keys - including one with a made up name and then no key - within seconds.

“Open source lets anyone build software without a big team,” Finkelshtein wrote in the Tuesday blog. “AI is doing the same for hacking. The skill is in the model, the model is a setting, and the person giving the instructions doesn't need to know how any of it works.” ®

evening.title: Microsoft refreshes Copilot app search for users without an AI subscription
evening.text:
Microsoft is updating search in its Microsoft 365 Copilot app for users without a Copilot license, with a toggle to restore the classic interface. Google, meanwhile, is giving AI searches more prominence on its homepage, where the familiar Search button is absent from a newly demonstrated layout.

Microsoft's change is rolling out now and will hit Deferred Release by mid-January 2027. It will impact users with a Microsoft 365 license who do not have a Copilot license and "provides modern search controls to help users find, refine, and navigate search results more easily."

It's enabled by default, which is a shame since administrators would likely prefer an opt-in rather than opt-out approach, and users can switch back to the "classic search experience" via a toggle on the search results page. Microsoft has not specified how long this toggle will remain available. Its separate Copilot Search experience had a fallback toggle scheduled for removal 60 days after general availability.

"With the updated search experience, users can continue to find files using keywords, use modern search controls to refine and navigate results, and search supported connected third-party content when their organization has configured connected sources," Microsoft said.

The results will still only display content to which users have permission. Microsoft advises administrators to brief users and help desks on the changed interface and the option to switch back.

Microsoft's search tweaks arrive as the future of the Google Search button on Google's desktop homepage looks uncertain.

In a post, Google VP of Product Robby Stein described a collapsible sidebar that lists users' recent AI conversations, pushing AI deeper into the search experience. Stein called it "a much simpler way to pick up where you left off," and said it would help customers "easily find & jump back into your recent AI searches."

However, something else was obvious in Stein's post: the Google Search button was not present.

Stein explained in August that Google had performed a "small test on desktop to help people find new things they can do with Search." Part of that test was the removal of the Google Search button.

Users can still submit queries by pressing Enter. Stein said the test would have "no impact to how the core search works."

The sidebar rollout doesn't itself confirm the Search button's permanent retirement. For now, its absence from Stein's demonstration is another sign of which features Google wants users to notice. ®

evening.title: Trump Raises Nuclear Alarm Over China a Day After Meeting Xi Jinping
evening.text:
Beijing is building nuclear weapons at a “hot and heavy” pace, President Donald Trump said, a day after he met Chinese leader Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin and the three countries agreed to talks on preventing nuclear proliferation.
While Russia and the US lead the world by each possessing thousands of nuclear weapons, China is rapidly expanding its nuclear arsenal.
In its annual review of China’s military buildup, the Pentagon said China’s stockpile of nuclear warheads remained in the low 600s through 2024, but the country was on track to have more than 1,000 warheads by 2030.
“They’ll catch us within 10 years,” Trump said of China’s nuclear buildup during a news conference at the White House on Friday. “They’re going at it hot and heavy, but they have a lot.” Trump’s public remarks were his first since his controversial summit with Xi and Putin, leaders of countries long considered US rivals, in the southern Chinese city of Shenzhen on Thursday. Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who spoke to reporters alongside Trump on Friday, said it was imperative for the three nuclear powers to talk.
“These three countries possess the overwhelming majority of nuclear weapons on this planet,” Rubio said. “The idea that these three leaders should not engage on a regular basis is not just absurd, it’s dangerous.” After the trilateral meeting, the leaders issued a joint statement, saying they “affirmed that a nuclear war cannot be won and must never be fought” and “will conduct a dialogue on reducing nuclear risks and preventing the proliferation of nuclear weapons”.
Prior to the meeting, observers had doubted if China would agree to nuclear talks. With a much smaller nuclear arsenal, Beijing had resisted joining nuclear arms control talks with the US and Russia.

evening.title: Porsche 718 Boxster prototype drive: This electric roadster is real
evening.text:
Porsche provided flights from Albany, New York, to Los Angeles and accommodation so Ars could drive the 718 EV prototype. Ars does not accept paid editorial content.

It wasn't until I was stuck in traffic on the way back from a run up and down some canyon roads that I realized just how low Porsche's upcoming all-electric 718 Boxster truly is. I was idly looking around at the other cars, doing the math on the EV adoption rate in this small sample of Los Angeles gridlock (roughly 50 percent, impressively) when I noticed that I was eye-level with a Tesla Model Y door handle.

That's not particularly low for a sports car, but it's practically unheard of for an EV. Nearly all modern electric cars are built atop a skateboard-style battery pack, a stack of cells that elevates the seating position by a good 3 inches. In these SUV-heady days, that's usually not a problem, possibly even an advantage. But, in a car like this, the closer you can get your keister to the road, the greater the sensation of speed.

So, for the company's first all-electric sports car, the 718 Boxster that will be fully revealed next year, Porsche engineers put the battery pack behind the driver. That powers a single motor spinning the rear wheels and creates a driving experience that both honors the simple joy of motoring in a mid-engined Boxster while pushing the 718 to new heights of power and performance.

evening.title: Homo erectus lived in the rainforest alongside Denisovans
evening.text:
Homo erectus was walking around mainland Asia at least 60,000 years more recently than archaeologists thought. A handful of teeth from two caves in southern China's Guangxi Province just filled in a significant gap in the fossil record of a region that's vital to the story of how our genus, Homo, took over the world.

The chemical makeup of the teeth's enamel suggests that, over the course of their lives, these Homo erectus moved across surprisingly large distances and made their living in dense tropical rainforests—an environment we'd previously assumed that only our species had ever gained a real foothold in. And one of the teeth offers a strong clue that Homo erectus probably shared this vast landscape with the Denisovans.

A handful of teeth with a lot to say

Baxian and Naxian are a pair of limestone caves that lie 15 kilometers apart along a karst valley corridor in southern China. University of Copenhagen paleoanthropologist Frido Welker and his colleagues unearthed a total of nine hominin teeth from among the more than 18,000 bones and fragments from non-hominin animals found there. Macquarie University paleoanthropologist Kira Westaway and her colleagues analyzed proteins and chemical isotopes from the enamel of five of these teeth.

evening.title: Microsoft brings serverless PostgreSQL into Fabric to bridge transactions and analytics
evening.text:
Microsoft has brought its HorizonDB PostgreSQL service into public preview in Fabric, aiming to bring transactional and analytical workloads closer together.

The corporation says applications can submit queries through a single PostgreSQL endpoint, with transactional and analytical work handled by the appropriate engines.

Analysts said the move follows similar efforts by Databricks and Snowflake to combine operational databases with analytics. But tighter integration with Microsoft's stack could make applications harder to move elsewhere.

Fabric HorizonDB joins SQL database and Cosmos DB in Microsoft's Fabric database portfolio. "By bringing operational databases, analytics, and AI together on a unified, governed platform, developers can build intelligent applications with less data movement and complexity. Fabric HorizonDB will also serve as the PostgreSQL backend for Fabric apps," Microsoft said.

Microsoft first unveiled Azure HorizonDB in preview in November 2025 and made it generally available last week. It competes with other cloud database services and distributed systems such as CockroachDB and YugabyteDB, both of which support PostgreSQL's wire protocol.

At the time, it said HorizonDB would offer "massive read scale without the need to replicate the database between instances."

Speaking to The Register last week, Shireesh Thota, veep of Azure databases and Fabric applications, said that bringing the system into Fabric – its platform for data lakes, data warehouses, and analytics launched in 2023 – would connect operational data in HorizonDB with analytical data in OneLake, Fabric's unified data lake.

"Once the data hits the OneLake storage, you can have analytical engines that take advantage of it. In HorizonDB, the PostgreSQL query engine can talk to the distributed query engine that we use in our Fabric data warehouse. We're fusing these query engines, thereby enabling the developers to submit a query that has pieces of the query that can work on OLTP and pieces of the query that can work on OLAP," he said.

"The application need not worry about two endpoints, or about consistency of data and all that complexity. They can just talk to HorizonDB as a Fabric endpoint, and they can submit all these queries. We are basically operationalizing in OneLake."

Operational data remains in HorizonDB's database storage, while mirroring maintains an analytical copy in OneLake, introduced in 2023, which replicates a snapshot of the external database to OneLake in Delta Parquet tables and keeps the replica synced in "near real time."

Thota said the process would not affect the transactional system. "Our core goal is to never impact OLTP workload while we are doing this, and we succeed [by] reading off the log as an additional replica to do this mirroring," he said.

But the overall plan of putting serverless PostgreSQL OLTP in an analytics platform, bringing it close to OLAP systems, is one some vendors are already executing to meet the demands of new AI agent-led workloads.

Adam Ronthal, research veep in Gartner's Data and Analytics Group, said: "The addition of Microsoft Fabric HorizonDB follows the 2025 acquisitions of PostgreSQL vendors by Databricks – Neon – and Snowflake – Crunchy. It delivers a high-performance, serverless operational RDBMS that is tightly coupled with Microsoft's lakehouse offering and well-suited to the ephemeral demands of AI agents.

"Competing directly with AWS Aurora and Google Cloud's AlloyDB, HorizonDB acts as a foundational serving layer for the next generation of AI- and analytics-infused applications. For organizations aligned with Azure and Fabric, it provides an industry-standard PostgreSQL foundation for AI development."

Andrew Snodgrass, research vice president of analyst company Directions on Microsoft, said the announcement of HorizonDB in Fabric was a "surprise," although "a watered-down version" compared to the version of the serverless database that became generally available on Azure last week. "It joins (document database) CosmosDB in Fabric and SQL database (based on the SQL Server engine) in Fabric. It highlights that Microsoft is still focused on making Fabric the data hub of their universe."

HorizonDB – both in Azure and Fabric – is a PostgreSQL service which Microsoft says has 100 percent compatibility with the open source system that has enjoyed a meteoric rise over the last decade. The support for PostgreSQL has led some to question the software giant's commitment to its own proprietary OLTP system, SQL Server.

Thota pointed out that the SQL database, based on the SQL Server engine, is already available in Fabric. Microsoft is also evaluating similar integration for that service, although he gave no timetable. "We are just beginning this journey, and most of the innovation is neutral to PostgreSQL and SQL. Some of it would be particular to how the individual query engine fuses with the analytical query engine. PostgreSQL does it slightly differently than SQL, but the idea is that most of the work is neutral. We are evaluating that work as well. I don't have timelines for that, but it is certainly in our thinking," he said.

Nonetheless, Holger Mueller, principal analyst at Constellation Research, said it was good to see Microsoft go all in on support of open source. "In general, it is an acknowledgement that they cannot win the battle for the SQL database with SQL Server – as it is as proprietary as the leader Oracle – and now they bank on the openness of PostgreSQL as another approach," he said.

However, using HorizonDB integrated into the Fabric/Azure stack may create so many dependencies with Microsoft's technology that lock-in to the vendor will remain a risk. "The primary concerns of open source – scale and support – have been eliminated by Microsoft's commitment and by now track record... the challenges are the embeddings of HorizonDB into the bigger Microsoft stack – which will make portability hard again. But every vendor wants and provides stickiness – clothed in ease of use and lower TCO," Mueller said. ®

evening.title: Home Ministry Warns of WhatsApp Web Risks Amid Pakistan Espionage Concerns
evening.text:
The Union Home Ministry’s nodal cyber security agency I4C has cautioned government functionaries against sharing sensitive information through WhatsApp Web sessions, a move that follows detection of suspicious activities of ‘Pakistan-based intelligence operatives’.
The cybersecurity advisory cautioning against using WhatsApp Web for official or sensitive work follows a probe that revealed Pakistan-based intelligence operatives infiltrated over 50 defence-related WhatsApp groups, said an official source on Monday.
Advising government officials to avoid staying logged in on computers and laptops, the National Cybercrime Threat Analytics Unit (NCTAU), Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre (I4C), warned that such sessions could be misused to take control of the account for fraud or phishing, said an official statement.
Sources said the Pakistan-based intelligence operatives used spoofed Indian numbers to join as ‘dead members’, monitoring chats in groups linked to the NSG, CRPF, commandos, and even DRDO without drawing attention.
Indian security agencies have now directed audits to remove unverified members of WhatsApp groups.
The I4C observed that an authenticated WhatsApp Web session may, under certain circumstances, be misused to gain unauthorised access to a user’s WhatsApp account.
Such unauthorised access may allow a malicious person to read messages, send messages while impersonating the user, access contacts and group conversations, and misuse the trusted identity of the account holder for fraud, phishing, social engineering or other malicious activities, said I4C in the statement.
“The users are, therefore, advised to exercise caution while using WhatsApp Web, particularly on office computers, shared systems, public computers or devices that may be accessible to other persons,” said the statement.
The I4C advisory also suggested precautionary measures like logging out after each session or using incognito/private browsing mode when use is unavoidable.
“Government, organisational, financial, confidential or other sensitive information should preferably not be exchanged through WhatsApp Web session on computers,” it said.
The MHA also advised officials to avoid leaving an authenticated WhatsApp Web session active when it is not required, particularly on office or shared computers.
Other tips the Ministry shared include avoiding unknown or public computers. “Do not log in to WhatsApp Web from cyber cafes, public kiosks, hotel business centres, borrowed computers or other untrusted systems,” it said.
The I4C also asked government functionaries to stay alert and watch for unusual account activity. “Unexpected messages sent from your account, unusual replies from contacts or unexplained activity should be treated seriously,” it said.
The advisory also asked officials to keep their device secure. “Keep the operating system, browser and security software updated, and avoid suspicious downloads, unknown files and cracked software,” said the I4C.
Source: IANS

evening.title: INS Sahyadri Completes Port Visit to Vietnam’s Da Nang During Far East Deployment
evening.text:
The Indian Navy’s indigenous guided-missile stealth frigate INS Sahyadri concluded its port visit to Da Nang in Vietnam from November 20 to 22 as part of its operational deployment to the Far East, the Ministry of Defence said on Monday.
“During the visit, the ship undertook professional and cultural engagements aimed at strengthening bilateral naval cooperation and fostering mutual understanding. These included interactions with senior leadership of the Vietnam People’s Navy, cross-visits by personnel of both navies and cultural exchanges,” the ministry said in a statement.
According to the MoD, the engagements provided opportunities to strengthen professional ties, mutual trust and camaraderie between the two navies.
“INS Sahyadri’s visit underscores the Indian Navy’s continued efforts to strengthen maritime partnerships and enhance cooperation with friendly foreign navies, in consonance with India’s Act East Policy and vision of MAHASAGAR (Mutual and Holistic Advancement for Security and Growth Across Regions),” the statement added.
The frigate had arrived at Tien Sa Port in Da Nang city on Friday for a three-day goodwill visit aimed at deepening defence ties and strengthening naval cooperation between India and Vietnam.
“The ship was accorded a warm welcome by the Vietnam People’s Navy and local authorities. The visit reaffirms our shared commitment to peace, stability and security in the region and in the Indo-Pacific,” the Indian Embassy in Vietnam had posted on X.
Earlier this month, a four-member delegation of the Vietnam People’s Army visited the College of Military Engineering (CME) in Pune, as part of the Subject Matter Expert Exchange (SMEE) programme.
“The visit focused on sharing expertise in combat engineering, counter-IED operations, HADR and engineering support to UN Peacekeeping Missions. The engagement further strengthened professional ties, mutual understanding and bilateral military cooperation between India and Vietnam,” the Indian Army had posted on X.
Recently, National Security Advisor (NSA) Ajit Doval was on an official visit to Vietnam, where he called on Vietnamese President To Lam and thanked him for his ‘steadfast support in strengthening the India-Vietnam Enhanced Comprehensive Strategic Partnership’.
Before arriving in Vietnam, INS Sahyadri participated in Exercise Malabar 2026 off Japan and departed Yokosuka Naval Base on November 12 following the conclusion of the exercise.

evening.title: Raising the stakes for enterprise networks with AI modernization
evening.text:
Enterprise networks are under severe strain. As companies rush to deploy artificial intelligence, the technology is quickly becoming the biggest source of demand on the network. Now, agentic AI is adding to the load. Tasks conducted by AI agents generate an estimated 450% more network traffic than the same tasks done by human workers.

As AI inference shifts from hyperscale training clouds—the huge centralized data centers where raw AI models ingest vast datasets and learn—to real-time, latency-sensitive applications, the need for on-premises or near-premises infrastructure grows. As a result, the gap between enterprise networks that are ready to support AI and those that are not is widening. As few as half of enterprises believe their current networks can handle AI’s bandwidth and latency demands, according to a recent study.

DOWNLOAD THE REPORT

This report explores how treating network modernization as an on-going strategy rather than a one-off project can help organizations adapt in the face of disruption and uncertainty.

Key findings from the report include:

AI may force companies to shift from a cloud-first approach to routing workloads. Training AI requires server-to-server data center architectures, while inference calls for low-latency connectivity close to users. Enterprises may need to fundamentally reconsider their network architecture to meet these requirements.

AI inference is pushing infrastructure back on premises. Inference typically requires real-time processing and is sensitive to latency, making hosting such capabilities on distant hyperscale clouds neither economical nor practical. Inconsistent latency can lead to AI model failures, driving up queue wait times, saturating GPUs loads, and causing bottlenecks in data flows. Large enterprises may need on-premises or near-premises inference, which reverses years of cloud-first consolidation and forces new approaches to data center architecture, connectivity, and physical infrastructure.

AI workloads are stressing physical network capacity in unexpected ways. The traffic increase from agentic AI, combined with inference moving on-premises, is exposing bandwidth bottlenecks in legacy underlay infrastructure.

Network modernization is an ongoing project that requires a holistic approach, allowing companies to adapt with ease. A combination of strong architectural governance, reusable design templates, and retained internal expertise supports organizations in adapting to disruptive events without rebuilding their infrastructure from scratch each time. Such events could include mergers and acquisitions, changing vendors, or technology upgrades.

NaaS and AI-driven observability can improve efficiency and reduce complexity in network operations. Network-as-a-service (NaaS) and AI-driven observability can offer companies benefits like faster, more flexible provisioning and lower costs.

Data sovereignty and sovereign AI will create infrastructure challenges for global enterprises. Regulators worldwide are passing laws requiring data and AI processing to remain within national borders. This conflicts with how multinational companies currently operate, requiring the build-out of sovereign-capable infrastructure for each geography, which will require significant new investment and complicate operations.

evening.title: US blacklists Megaspeed hours after Jensen Huang returns to Nvidia
evening.text:
Jensen Huang was barely back in charge of Nvidia when Uncle Sam slapped Megaspeed –­ the Singaporean cloud provider at the center of the scandal that cost him his job ­­– on its trade blacklist.

The US Department of Commerce's Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) has added Megaspeed and a number of affiliated businesses to its Entity List, restricting their access to American technology amid an ongoing investigation into the suspected diversion of advanced GPUs to China.

The final rule [PDF], filed Monday afternoon and scheduled for publication in the Federal Register on Wednesday, names seven businesses across Singapore, Malaysia, and Thailand, including Megaspeed's owner, Swiftdata, and Malaysian subsidiary Speedmatrix.

Also in Washington's crosshairs is Apex Enterprise Solutions, a Singapore-based subsidiary of Chinese cloud computing giant Alibaba.

BIS said the businesses posed a significant risk of diverting advanced computing hardware to recipients or applications not authorized by the US government. Anyone looking to supply the seven companies with goods subject to US export controls will need a license, with applications subject to a "presumption of denial."

Despite the timing of Monday's announcement, the US government's interest in Megaspeed predates the revelations about Jensen Huang's private life by some considerable margin.

In a joint statement issued last week, the Departments of Justice and Commerce confirmed that the latter had opened an investigation into Megaspeed in 2024 after spotting suspicious activity while monitoring potential violations of semiconductor export controls.

Investigators requested records from Nvidia relating to both direct and indirect sales to Megaspeed in May 2025, and the GPU giant put the Singaporean outfit on its internal "no sell" list the following month. US investigators, accompanied by Singaporean law enforcement officials, subsequently visited Megaspeed's premises and interviewed its then-CEO, Alice Huang.

The Justice Department has since taken the lead on the criminal investigation.

Alice Huang, who is not related to the Nvidia boss, is a businesswoman with whom Jensen was said to be having an affair – he admitted to extramarital infidelity earlier this month, although he never name-checked the Megaspeed exec. According to reports, US intelligence officials suspected she was working on behalf of Chinese intelligence, though Beijing has rejected the espionage allegations.

Megaspeed maintains that its business is lawful and says Alice Huang formally left the company in August last year. It has also enlisted outside lawyers to conduct an internal investigation.

Nvidia's own Huang lasted all of 11 days in corporate exile. The chipmaker's board unanimously voted to reinstate its co-founder as president and CEO on Monday, less than a week after board chairman Harvey Jones indicated that bringing him back wasn't on the cards.

The U-turn followed a lobbying campaign by some of Silicon Valley's biggest names, including Elon Musk, and some rather more consequential intervention from the White House. President Donald Trump told CNBC on Monday that he had personally persuaded Nvidia's directors to give Huang his job back.

Nvidia's board said it had received assurances from senior US government officials regarding the national security implications of Huang's return.

There are still plenty of people in Washington who have questions for Huang, however. The Nvidia boss is due to sit down with three congressional committees on December 1, with the chipmaker's general counsel, Tim Teter, scheduled to face lawmakers the following day.

Nvidia has also established a board-level committee to oversee national security and export control compliance, putting its trade compliance personnel under the supervision of three directors.

Nvidia shareholders may be delighted to have Jensen back, but the returning CEO has barely a week to prepare for his congressional grilling over the affair that helped bring about his departure. ®
